plain: A slender muscle lying on the front of psoas major. It is absent in about 40 per cent of people.
detail: From the bodies of T12 and L1 to the pectineal line and iliopubic eminence. Supplied by L1.
clinical: A weak flexor of the trunk, and one of the commonest normal anatomical variants — do not read its absence as pathology.

plain: A long thick muscle from the lumbar spine to the top of the thigh bone — the deepest muscle of the back wall of the abdomen and the strongest hip flexor.
detail: From the transverse processes, bodies and discs of T12–L5, passing under the inguinal ligament to the lesser trochanter, joined by iliacus. Supplied by the anterior rami of L1–L3.
clinical: The lumbar plexus forms within its substance. Irritation — from appendicitis or a psoas abscess — causes pain on passive hip extension, the psoas sign.

plain: A fan-shaped muscle inside the pelvis that turns sharply through a right angle to reach the hip, like a rope over a pulley.
detail: From the inner surface of the obturator membrane and surrounding bone, leaving the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen and turning laterally to the greater trochanter. Supplied by the nerve to obturator internus (L5, S1).
clinical: It forms the lateral wall of the ischio-anal fossa, where the pudendal nerve and vessels run in its fascia within the pudendal (Alcock's) canal.

plain: A muscle on the outer surface of the obturator membrane that spirals behind the hip joint to reach the femur.
detail: From the outer surface of the obturator membrane and its bony margins to the trochanteric fossa of the femur. Supplied by the obturator nerve — unlike the other short lateral rotators.
clinical: Its obturator nerve supply marks it out from the rest of the short rotators, which come from sacral plexus branches.

plain: Two small twin muscles above and below the tendon of obturator internus, reinforcing its pull.
detail: Superior gemellus from the ischial spine, inferior from the ischial tuberosity, both blending with the obturator internus tendon to reach the greater trochanter.
clinical: With piriformis, obturator internus and quadratus femoris they form the short lateral rotator group, which stabilises the hip in single-leg stance.

plain: A small triangular sheet at the back of the pelvic floor, running from the bony spine of the pelvis to the tailbone.
detail: From the ischial spine to the lateral margin of the coccyx and lower sacrum, lying on the sacrospinous ligament. With levator ani it forms the pelvic diaphragm. Supplied by S4 and S5.
clinical: It supports the pelvic viscera and pulls the coccyx forwards after defecation or childbirth.

plain: The long thin strap running down the inner thigh — the most superficial of the adductors, and the only one crossing the knee.
detail: From the body and inferior ramus of the pubis to the upper medial tibia as part of the pes anserinus. Supplied by the obturator nerve.
clinical: Because it is expendable and has a single reliable neurovascular pedicle, gracilis is a favourite muscle for free flap transfer and for reconstructing a facial or anal sphincter.

plain: The longest muscle in the body, ribboning diagonally across the front of the thigh from the hip point to the inner knee.
detail: From the anterior superior iliac spine to the upper medial tibia in the pes anserinus. Supplied by the femoral nerve.
clinical: It flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the hip while flexing the knee — the cross-legged tailor's position that gives it its name. Its medial border forms the lateral boundary of the femoral triangle, and it roofs the adductor canal.

plain: A short adductor lying behind pectineus and adductor longus.
detail: From the body and inferior ramus of the pubis to the upper linea aspera. Supplied by the obturator nerve.
clinical: The two divisions of the obturator nerve straddle it — the anterior branch in front, the posterior behind — which makes it the key landmark for identifying them.

ta2: Musculus vastus lateralis; Musculus vastus intermedius
plain: The outer and the deep central parts of the quadriceps. Together with the other two they straighten the knee.
detail: Vastus lateralis from the greater trochanter and lateral linea aspera; vastus intermedius from the anterior and lateral shaft of the femur. Both join the quadriceps tendon. Supplied by the femoral nerve.
clinical: Vastus lateralis is the preferred intramuscular injection site in infants, being bulky and free of major vessels and nerves.

plain: Two of the three long columns of the erector spinae running either side of the spine — the outer and the middle.
detail: Iliocostalis is the most lateral column, attaching to the ribs; longissimus is intermediate, running to the transverse processes and mastoid. Both arise from the erector spinae aponeurosis and are supplied by the posterior rami.
clinical: Remember the three columns from lateral to medial as 'I Love Spine' — Iliocostalis, Longissimus, Spinalis.

plain: The nerve of the inner thigh. It leaves the pelvis through a canal in the obturator foramen to supply the adductor muscles.
detail: From the lumbar plexus (L2–L4). Passes through the obturator canal and divides into anterior and posterior branches around adductor brevis, supplying the adductor group and skin over the medial thigh.
clinical: Because it also supplies the hip joint, hip disease can refer pain to the medial thigh and knee — and it is why knee pain in a child may actually be a slipped femoral epiphysis.

plain: The largest branch of the lumbar plexus. It enters the thigh beside the femoral artery and supplies the muscles that straighten the knee.
detail: L2–L4. Descends between psoas major and iliacus, passing under the inguinal ligament LATERAL to the femoral artery — outside the femoral sheath. Supplies iliacus, the quadriceps, sartorius and pectineus, and skin over the anterior thigh via the saphenous nerve.
clinical: Remember the order in the femoral triangle from lateral to medial as NAVEL — Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics. Injury abolishes knee extension and the knee jerk.

plain: The two nerves of the buttock muscles, named for whether they pass above or below piriformis.
detail: The superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1) leaves above piriformis to supply gluteus medius, minimus and tensor fasciae latae; the inferior (L5–S2) leaves below it to supply gluteus maximus.
clinical: Superior gluteal nerve injury gives a positive Trendelenburg sign, because gluteus medius can no longer keep the pelvis level. It is at risk in a badly placed intramuscular injection, which is why the upper outer quadrant is used.

meshNames: Posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh.r
en: Posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh
plain: A purely sensory nerve supplying the skin over the back of the thigh, down as far as the calf.
detail: From S1–S3, leaving the pelvis below piriformis and running deep to gluteus maximus, then superficially down the back of the thigh.
clinical: It gives the longest cutaneous territory in the lower limb, and its gluteal branches supply the skin over the lower buttock.

plain: A small nerve running through the inguinal canal to supply the skin of the upper inner thigh and the external genitalia.
detail: From L1. Pierces the abdominal wall muscles, traverses the inguinal canal and emerges through the superficial inguinal ring — it does not pass through the deep ring.
clinical: The nerve most often injured in inguinal hernia repair or a Pfannenstiel incision, producing numbness and sometimes persistent neuropathic groin pain.

plain: The main vessels running along the pelvic brim to the groin, where they become the femoral vessels.
detail: The external iliac artery arises from the common iliac at the sacro-iliac joint and becomes the femoral artery at the inguinal ligament. It gives the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac arteries just before it does.
clinical: The inferior epigastric artery is the landmark that separates hernia types: an indirect hernia enters lateral to it, a direct hernia bulges medial to it.

plain: The main artery and vein of the thigh, running down from the groin inside a fascial sleeve.
detail: The femoral artery begins at the mid-inguinal point and passes down the femoral triangle and adductor canal to the adductor hiatus, where it becomes the popliteal artery. The vein lies medial to it at the groin.
clinical: The femoral pulse is felt at the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis. The vein just medial to it is the standard route for central venous access and cardiac catheterisation.

meshNames: 1th to 4th perforating branches of the deep femoral artery.r
en: Deep artery of the thigh & its perforators
plain: The large branch of the femoral artery that dives deep to supply the thigh muscles, sending branches straight through the adductor magnus.
detail: Arises from the femoral artery a few centimetres below the inguinal ligament, gives the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries, then four perforating branches that pierce adductor magnus to supply the posterior compartment.
clinical: The medial circumflex femoral artery is the main blood supply to the head of the femur in adults, which is why an intracapsular neck fracture threatens the head with avascular necrosis.

plain: A branch of the internal iliac artery running with the obturator nerve out of the pelvis to the inner thigh.
detail: Usually from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, passing through the obturator canal. Gives an acetabular branch that runs in the ligament of the head of the femur.
clinical: In around a fifth of people it arises instead from the inferior epigastric artery and curves round the femoral ring — the 'corona mortis', which can bleed alarmingly during femoral hernia repair.

plain: A sheet closing most of the large opening in the hip bone, leaving a small canal at the top for vessels and a nerve.
detail: Fills the obturator foramen except superiorly, where its free margin and the obturator groove form the obturator canal. Gives attachment to obturator internus and externus.

plain: A band of fascia dividing the space under the inguinal ligament into two compartments — one for muscle, one for vessels.
detail: Runs from the inguinal ligament to the iliopubic eminence, separating the muscular lacuna (iliopsoas and femoral nerve) laterally from the vascular lacuna (femoral vessels) medially.
clinical: This division is why a psoas abscess and a femoral hernia present in different places below the inguinal ligament.

plain: The joint between the lower end of the sacrum and the tailbone, with a small disc between them.
detail: A secondary cartilaginous joint with a fibrocartilaginous disc, reinforced by anterior, posterior and lateral sacrococcygeal ligaments, with the intercornual ligaments joining the cornua.
clinical: It allows the coccyx to move backwards during childbirth, enlarging the pelvic outlet. Forced flexion in a fall onto the buttocks causes coccydynia.

meshNames: 1th to 4th perforating branches of the deep femoral vein.r
en: Deep veins of the lower limb
plain: The large veins running alongside the arteries deep in the thigh and pelvis, carrying most of the blood back from the leg.
detail: The femoral vein continues from the popliteal vein at the adductor hiatus, receives the deep femoral vein and the great saphenous vein, and becomes the external iliac vein at the inguinal ligament. It lies medial to the artery at the groin and posterior to it in the adductor canal.
clinical: These are the veins of deep vein thrombosis, and the source of most pulmonary emboli. Their valves are what normally stop blood pooling; failure of the perforator valves is what makes superficial veins varicose.

plain: A small band joining the horn-like projections of the sacrum and the coccyx at the very base of the spine.
detail: Connects the sacral cornua to the coccygeal cornua, bridging the sides of the sacral hiatus.
clinical: The sacral cornua it joins are the landmark palpated to find the sacral hiatus for a caudal epidural block.

plain: A superficial vein of the thigh running alongside the great saphenous vein and joining it near the groin.
detail: Drains the anteromedial thigh and joins the great saphenous vein close to the saphenofemoral junction.
clinical: A frequent site of recurrent varicose veins after surgery, because it is easily missed at the saphenofemoral junction.
